title: Seven days
hook: Maya dies a week after the birth; her sister Mahapajapati raises him as her own

segments.voice: Yesterday: the old sage weeps. Asita held the baby and cried because he'd never hear him teach. Your line was plant it anyway. What did you plant? Day twenty-five.
screen: `THE OLD SAGE WEEPS — PLANT IT ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: So far the story has been all wonders. A shining elephant in a dream. A branch bending down to a queen's hand. Gods cheering in the sky. An old sage in tears of joy. It feels like a fairy tale. And then, one week in, the story does something fairy tales usually don't. It breaks your heart. Seven days after the birth, Queen Maya dies. The baby who everyone says will change the world is one week old, and he has no mother.
screen: `WONDERS, ONE AFTER ANOTHER.` → `THEN, ONE WEEK IN.` → `THE BABY HAS NO MOTHER.`

segments.voice: The oldest discourses say it plainly, as if it were simply part of the pattern. Seven days after a future buddha is born, his mother dies. That's all. No long scene. The later tradition softens it a little: Maya, it says, is reborn in a heaven, and one story tells of the Buddha, years later, going to teach her there. But on earth, a newborn has lost his mother. And here's who steps in. Maya's younger sister, Mahapajapati Gotami. She's also married to King Suddhodana, which was not unusual for a royal house then. She has a baby of her own, a son, Nanda. And the texts say she gives her own son to nurses, and nurses Siddhattha herself. She raises him as her own. Years later, the Buddha remembers it. In one discourse, when Mahapajapati tries to give him a gift, he tells his attendant Ananda that she has done so much for him. She was his aunt, his foster mother, his nurse. She suckled him when his mother died. That's the Buddha saying thank you, in public, for being raised. And Mahapajapati's own story doesn't end there. She'll come back later on this path, as someone who changes the whole community forever. But today is just about this: a child whose first great loss came before he could remember it, and a woman who chose to love him as if he were hers. The tradition keeps them both. The mother who carried him. And the mother who raised him.
screen: `SEVEN DAYS AFTER THE BIRTH.` · `MAHAPAJAPATI STEPS IN.` · `SHE NURSED HIM HERSELF.` · `THE BUDDHA REMEMBERS IT.` · then, large: `LOVE CAN BE ADOPTED.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Let the breath settle. Then think of someone who raised you, or part of you. A parent, a grandparent, a stepparent, an aunt, a coach, a teacher, a neighbor who fed you. Anyone who did some of the raising, whether or not they had to. Picture their face. Thank them silently. If that relationship is complicated, that's okay: you can thank the part that helped, and leave the rest. The bell holds the time.
Seven days. Queen Maya died a week after the birth, and her sister Mahapajapati raised the child as her own.
Your line: love can be adopted. Today, notice someone caring for a child, an animal, or a person who isn't theirs by birth, and honor it quietly. Day twenty-five.

screen: `DAY 25 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE ONE WHOSE AIM SUCCEEDS.`

howItsDone: Buddhists honor both Maya, the Buddha's mother, and Mahapajapati Gotami, who raised him; Mahapajapati is especially remembered as the first Buddhist nun, and many traditions stress gratitude to parents and those who raise us.

original.note: Pali: Mahāpajāpatī, 'great leader of many'; Gotamī is her clan name.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha had a charmed royal childhood.
what it means: his mother died when he was a week old, and his aunt raised him as her own.

what a scholar hears: the Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta (MN 123) states the seven-day pattern; the Dakkhinavibhanga Sutta (MN 142) records the Buddha's thanks to Mahapajapati, who later became the first bhikkhuni.

sources.ref: Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 123): the mother dies seven days after the birth
Dakkhinavibhanga Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 142): the Buddha remembers Mahapajapati's care

notes: Maya's rebirth in Tusita heaven (MN 123) is given as 'a heaven'; the Buddha teaching his mother (in Tavatimsa, in the Abhidhamma tradition) is mentioned as 'one story'. Confirm framing.
Mahapajapati giving her son Nanda to nurses: from the commentaries (Nidanakatha / Theri Apadana); confirm.
Meaning of the name Mahapajapati in the original note ('great leader of many') is uncertain; a Keeper should confirm or remove.
Her role as the first nun is only hinted at ('she'll come back later on this path').
